To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The lifetime of a protein crystal can be extended by reducing the exposure time and using a fast detector.
The lifetime of room temperature macromolecular crystals can be increased by using a fast detector and by reducing the exposure time.

1) room-temperature crystallography is possible for a broad range of proteins and viruses; 2) the lifetime of room-temperature macomolecular crystals can be significantly extended by using a fast detector and reducing the exposure time; 3) the crystal lifetime is correlated to the size of the unit cell; and 4) the lifetime is not correlated to the size or shape of the crystal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the physical properties of materials and the development of new materials with improved properties.
the development and application of novel techniques for the investigation of the structure and dynamics of biological macromolecules.
the use of X-ray diffraction techniques to investigate the structure and function of proteins and viruses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of reduced exposures and fast detectors in macromolecular crystallo- graphy can lead to an increase in the lifetimes of room-temperature protein crystals, and thus an increase in the quality of diffraction data.
the X-ray beam is the main limiting factor for the lifetime of room-temperature protein crystals, and that this can be overcome by using a faster detector and a more intense X-ray beam.
room-temperature macromo-lecular crystallography can now be performed routinely and efficiently.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lifetime of room-temperature crystals has been extended from a few minutes to several days.
the use of a fast detector and reduced exposure times can extend the lifetime of a crystal by 10- to 100-fold.

we have developed and demonstrated a new approach to macromolecular crystal data collection that is compatible with the existing infrastructure and that has the potential for significantly improving data quality and reducing the time and effort needed for data collection.
The main takeaway from our work is that

room-temperature data collection is a practical alternative to cryogenic methods for macromolecular crystals, and the use of reduced exposures and fast detectors will be essential for the future success of room-temperature data-collection methods.
